title: Tree indexing: ISAM and B+ trees
lead: Build pages of signposts, insert one key and delete two others. Check the path of an actual search after each repair.
goals: Use separators to find a leaf and scan a range
Simulate insertion and deletion using the order-d convention
Explain copy-up, push-up, and byte-based occupancy

sections.title: Build a page of signposts before building a tree
sections.html:
A sorted file lets us discard half the search region at a time, but a large file still requires many unpredictable page jumps. Could one page tell us which smaller region contains a key? In an original example, put two leaf pages behind a root: left [4,9], right [12,15,18]. Store boundary 12 in the root. To find 15, compare with 12, choose the right child, then search that leaf. To find 10, choose the left and establish absence there. The root contains routing information; the leaves contain the data entries, which may be complete records or key/RID references as in the previous lesson.

                  [12]
            /         \
      [4,9]   ↔   [12,15,18]
       k<12          k≥12

One root can point to many children: the number of child pointers is its fanout. If its signposts themselves become too numerous, add another signpost level above them. A B+ tree keeps every leaf at the same depth, so an exact lookup follows one path of the same length to a leaf. Leaf links let a range lookup find its starting leaf and continue in key order. An equality lookup over duplicates must return every matching entry, even across leaf boundaries; our update traces use unique keys to make the movement easy to see.

To make updates checkable, choose the lecture’s order-d count convention. A non-root leaf contains d…2d data entries; a non-root internal node contains d…2d separator keys and therefore d+1…2d+1 child pointers. The root is allowed exceptions: an internal root normally has at least two children; a root leaf can represent a small or empty tree. These bounds reserve room to repair growth and shrinkage. We will use d=2, hence a four-entry leaf limit, and check routing as well as occupancy after every change.

sections.title: Insert 15: why a leaf copies a key upward
sections.html:
Start earlier, with just one root leaf [4,9,12,18]. Insert 15 into its sorted position: [4,9,12,15,18]. Five entries exceed capacity four; we cannot merely add another root pointer without deciding which entries each pointer reaches. Split the ordered sequence, then create a parent that describes the resulting ranges.

StepLeft leafRight leafParent
Before insertion[4,9,12,18] (root leaf)——
Temporary overflow[4,9,12,15,18]——
Split[4,9][12,15,18]New root [12]
Check counts2 entries ≥d3 entries ≤2dTwo child pointers

The separator 12 says “keys below 12 go left; keys at least 12 go right”. Keep the original 12 in the right leaf: only that copy is a data entry. Copying it into the parent is called copy-up. If we removed it from the leaves, following the leaf chain would lose a real key. Link left and right leaves in both directions where supported. The tree gained one level because the old root split; a split below an existing root does not necessarily increase height.

Check an inclusive range 8…16. Descend toward 8 into [4,9], skip 4, output 9, follow the next-leaf link, output 12 and 15, then stop at 18 because all later keys are too large. The result [9,12,15] checks both routing and the leaf link.

Internal overflow needs a different action. Suppose an internal node temporarily has [10,20,30,40,50] and children C0…C5. Move middle boundary 30 into its parent. The left internal node keeps [10,20] with C0,C1,C2; the right keeps [40,50] with C3,C4,C5. This is push-up: 30 is removed from those two internal separator lists, while data entries in the leaves remain. The parent can now distinguish the two ranges. If it overflows, repeat upward. A sibling with spare space can sometimes accept redistributed entries instead, but associated pointers and boundaries must be updated too.

Key takeaway

Copy-up retains the data key in the leaf. The root’s copy of 12 is used for routing. The leaf must retain 12 so that a scan through the leaves reads all the data entries.

sections.title: Delete, then prove that searches still work
sections.html:
Use the tree after inserting 15: root [12], leaves [4,9] and [12,15,18], d=2. Delete 4. Left becomes [9], below its minimum. Right has three entries, so it can lend one and retain two. Move 12 left: leaves become [9,12] and [15,18]. Change the parent from [12] to [15]. A search for 12 now goes left; leaving boundary 12 unchanged would send it right and falsely report absence.

Next delete 9. Left is [12]; right has exactly two entries, so lending would make it underfull too. Merge into [12,15,18], which fits capacity four. Remove the redundant parent boundary and child pointer. The root now has only one child; replace it with that leaf, shortening the tree. A leaf merge does not insert the parent separator as another data record: 15 is already in the combined leaf.

After operationRootLeavesLookup check
Delete 4 and redistribute[15][9,12] ↔ [15,18]12 goes left; 15 goes right
Delete 9 and merge[12,15,18] (leaf)One leafAll three entries found directly

Internal repair also moves child ranges. Take a parent boundary 30, left internal keys [10,20] with C0,C1,C2 and underfull right keys [40] with C3,C4. Merge by pulling 30 down: [10,20,30,40] with C0,C1,C2,C3,C4. Without 30 the distinction between C2 and C3 is lost. Searching 25 should reach C2; searching 35 should reach C3. The parent loses a key and pointer, so it may require the same repair at the next level.

For internal redistribution, use a separate state: parent [40]; left [10,20,30] with D0…D3; underfull right [60] with D4,D5. Move D3 to the front of the right node, move parent 40 down there and move 30 up. Result: left [10,20]/D0,D1,D2; parent [30]; right [40,60]/D3,D4,D5. D3 still covers [30,40), and searching 35 still reaches it. Moving keys without children would break this invariant. Choose an adjacent sibling with the same parent; a neighbouring leaf in the linked chain may belong to another parent.

After redistributing the first leaf example, why is checking “both leaves have two entries” insufficient?

Reasoned answer. Occupancy checks capacity, not routing. The boundary must be 15 under our convention, and leaf links must still preserve order. Check every data entry, equal leaf depth, boundary ranges and occupancy; repair may propagate to ancestors.

Key takeaway

Redistributing a key also requires updating the parent’s separator. If the root still stores 12, a search for 12 goes right even though the record has moved left. Valid leaf occupancy alone does not guarantee correct lookup.

sections.title: Compare a growing tree with fixed signposts
sections.html:
Suppose a leaf responsible for [20,40) is full, then 27,28,29 arrive. A B+ tree can redistribute or split and update its routing structure. ISAM, Indexed Sequential Access Method, keeps the upper routing structure fixed and hangs overflow pages off the primary leaf. Its primary leaves are allocated in key order in the lecture’s model, while overflow entries need not be sorted. A lookup routes to a range, then checks that range’s overflow chain. Repeated inserts can lengthen the chain without adding tree levels. Deleting a boundary-valued record need not invalidate the fixed ISAM boundary: it still partitions the key space. Empty overflow pages can be reclaimed.

How shallow can many-way routing be? In an ideal full tree with fanout 100 and 1,000,000 leaf pages, three edges suffice because 100³=1,000,000. Counting root and leaves gives four levels. Actual page I/O depends on cached upper levels and whether the leaf contains records or RIDs requiring further fetches. Height is therefore not the whole query cost.

Our count rule also hides entry sizes. A 256-byte page must fit its header, pointers and key bytes; three long strings might fill it where ten short ones fit. Half the entries need not mean half the bytes. Some production deletion policies postpone rebalancing and reclaim only empty pages. Treat these policies separately from the textbook d…2d exercise.

Compression can improve fanout without losing routing. For leaf keys cat01,cat02,cat09, store common prefix cat0 once and suffixes 1,2,9; the original strings remain recoverable. Internal suffix truncation has another purpose: keep only enough of a boundary to separate ranges. Between left keys beginning apple and right keys beginning banana, separator b works under ordinary lexicographic order if every left key is below b and every right key is at least b. Arbitrarily reducing leaf keys to b would lose data.

The tree has short routing paths but a heavily updated ISAM range has five overflow pages. Can height alone compare their lookup costs?

Reasoned answer. No. Count the primary leaf and relevant overflow reads as well as upper-level reads and record fetches. A fixed upper structure keeps maintenance local but does not bound the growth of an overflow chain. For duplicate keys, also ensure the lookup visits every matching entry or RID list.

quiz.question: When the leaf [4,9,12,15,18] splits into [4,9] and [12,15,18], what happens to separator 12?
options: It is removed from every leaf
It is copied into the parent and retained in the right leaf
It is retained only in the left leaf
quiz.explanation: The right leaf starts at 12, so its parent boundary is 12. Copy that boundary into the parent but retain the data entry in the right leaf: a leaf-chain scan must still return 12. Internal-node splitting instead moves a separator up while preserving the leaf data.
